en: The Profound Meaning of the "Bodhisattva Ground Chapter" from the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Śrāmaṇera Zhixu of Ancient Wu;
Revised by the Bodhisattva Bhikṣu Daofang of Wénlíng.

Now, when the Way reaches the depths of the ocean of awakening, it must manifest compassion in accordance with the inherent nature; when the teachings reach all capacities, they must subsume the derivative to return to the fundamental.
Thus, while the internal and external realms appear distinct and cannot be harmonized, their sequential arrangement and perfect fusion are of a kind that knows no separation.
The "Mind-Ground Chapter" of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* is the original source of all sentient beings and the very life-force of the wisdom of all Buddhas.
Ah! Because its fundamental source and intrinsic nature are pure, it is called "Brahman" (梵). Because its life of wisdom pervades all lands and moments, it is called a "net" (網).

Because it is that from which the myriad dharmas arise and gather, it is called "mind" (心). Because it is that upon which both ordinary beings and sages rely and are sustained, it is called "ground" (地).
In terms of the person, Vairocana is the essence and Śākyamuni is the trace; in terms of the land, it is the Flower Treasury (華藏).
The fundamental [source] is the basis, and this realm is the trace. Although the fundamental and the trace differ, neither departs from the Brahma-net.
In terms of the Dharma, what is taught in the nine locations is the particular, while the four dhyānas now discussed are the general.

In terms of meaning, the successive stages of practice are the particular, while the initial resolve and the prātimokṣa are the general. Although the general and the particular differ, neither transcends the mind-ground. Therefore:
When the conditions were first ripe, he received the assembly to behold the original source; once the ground of the mind had unfolded, he maintained the Dharma to transmit it to other realms.
Manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment, he extensively expounded the particulars within the universal;

returning to Bodhi, he first laid out the universality within the particulars. How profound this teaching is! It is truly the essential ford for turning back from delusion and returning to awakening. Practice...
This is the very root of the Bodhisattva path. By examining a single chapter, one understands the essential purpose of an entire collection;

by understanding an entire collection, one penetrates the ritual methods of an entire era. By contemplating a single Buddha, one universally knows the models of the ten directions and the three periods of time.

Thus, one inherits the fragrant regulations of former sages and supplements what was incomplete in the teachings of past saints. Now, before explaining the scriptural text, I shall first present five [points].

The Meaning [of the Title]. This consists of five parts: first, the explanation of names; second, the manifestation of the essence; third, the clarification of the primary tenet; fourth, the discernment of its function;

and fifth, the characteristics of the teaching. The explanation of names has two sections: first, the explanation of the title of the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* spoken by the Buddha; second, the explanation of the title of the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Ground of the Mind.

The first section [the explanation of the title of the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*] has three parts: first, the explanation of "spoken by the Buddha" (*buddha-bhāṣita*); second, the explanation of "Brahmajāla"; and third, the explanation of "sūtra."

The initial statement "spoken by the Buddha" refers to the proclamation by the Great Sage, the Compassionate Honored One, through his fourfold eloquence. In the Sanskrit language, he is fully called *Buddha*;
this translates here as "the Awakened One. Because he has awakened himself, awakened others, and perfected the practice of awakening, he is named Buddha.

From the beginning to the end, this encompasses the meaning of the six stages of realization (*liu ji*): that all sentient beings inherently possess the nature of awakening is termed the "principle" (*li*).

The Buddha. Upon hearing this principle of nature, one’s perfect understanding first opens; this is the Buddha of Names. Moment by moment observing the mind and subduing the afflictions of the five abodes is called the Buddha of Contemplative Practice.
When the practice is profound and defilements fall away, purifying the six sense organs, it is called the Buddha of Similarity.

Partially breaking through ignorance and partially perceiving the dharma-nature is called the Buddha of Partial Realization. When ignorance is completely severed and the principle of nature is perfectly manifested, [one is the true Buddha].

This is called the ultimate Buddha. The Buddha has three bodies, namely: the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). The Dharma-body is the essential substance of original enlightenment (*mūlajñāna*).

The Reward-body is the perfection of the wisdom of initial enlightenment (*ādikṣāntijñāna*). The Transformation-body is the manifestation through compassion. In some places it is said that the Dharma-body is named Vairocana;
this translates as "Universal Radiance. The Reward-body is named Rocana; this translates as "Pure Fulfillment. The Transformation...
His name is Śākyamuni, which translates as "Able Sage" (Nengren) and "Silent One" (Jimo).
However, in the Jin translations of the *Avataṃsaka*, he is consistently called Rocana, while in the Tang translations, he is called Vairocana;

these are merely differences in the pronunciation of the Sanskrit sounds, and it is not necessarily the case that these terms exclusively distinguish between the Dharma-body and the Reward-body. Furthermore, in the *Avataṃsaka*, he is sometimes named Śākya and sometimes named Vairocana. Fundamentally...
There is no difference in essence. In this scripture, Vairocana sits upon his own lotus pedestal, while Śākyamuni presides over ten billion worlds.
One should know that the three bodies are neither identical nor different; they appear as one or as different only because the capacities and conditions of sentient beings differ.

Furthermore, each of the three bodies possesses both a simple and a composite meaning. As for the simple meaning of the Dharmakāya, it refers exclusively to the fundamentally pure principle-body. As for the Sambhogakāya...
The "single" refers exclusively to the supreme merit and wisdom. The "single" *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) refers exclusively to the manifested response, like the moon in water.

The "double" *dharmakāya* (dharma body) consists of two aspects: first, the *dharmakāya* of intrinsically pure nature, which is the original, self-sovereign Buddha of the fundamental source of all sentient beings;
second, the wondrously sublime *dharmakāya* free from defilement, which is that realized by all Buddhas.
This is the ultimate principle of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Regarding the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body), there are two types:
first, the self-enjoyment *saṃbhogakāya*, which is the ultimate, true fruit of the two virtues of wisdom and abandonment of all Buddhas;

second, the other-enjoyment *saṃbhogakāya*, which refers to the marks and signs perceived by Bodhisattvas on the stages according to their mental capacity—each and every mark and sign being without limit or division.

Regarding the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), there are two types: first, the response body (*sambhogakāya*), which manifests the eight phases of enlightenment; second, the emanation body (*nairmāṇikakāya*), which suddenly appears where it previously did not exist.
Furthermore, the transformation body is also called the response body, as it manifests in accordance with sentient beings, like the moon reflected in water.
Regarding the manifestation of the eight phases, there are again three kinds: first, the superior response body, which is seen by the great beings of the stages (*bhūmi*). Its characteristics are...

First, the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*), which is immeasurable and perceived by a certain class of beings with great roots; although they have not yet ascended to the [bodhisattva] stages, they are able to see it through the power of their roots of goodness.

This is also termed the "retributive enjoyment for others. Second, the Body Corresponding to Inferior and Superior Capacities (*hīnaviśiṣṭānuprāptakāya*), which is seen by the three vehicles of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*);

it is "superior" because it serves as an entry point into the Distinct and Perfect Teachings, yet it is "inferior" because it still relies on the consciousness of phenomena (*vastu-vijñāna*). Third, the Inferior...
The *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is that which is perceived by those of dull faculties within the realm as the form of an old bhikṣu sixteen feet tall.
Because it relies solely on the functioning of the *vastu-vijñāna* (consciousness of objects) and fails to penetrate the boundless significance of the ocean of marks, it is termed "inferior.

Regarding these three types of *nirmāṇakāyas*, their characteristics must further be distinguished according to the horizontal and vertical dimensions. To distinguish them horizontally, they are simply the sixteen-foot objective bodies fixed within the realm.

Those of dull faculties within the realm perceive him sitting beneath a wooden tree on a seat of living grass; with the body of an aged bhikṣu, he turns the wheel of the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing.
Those of sharp faculties within the realm see him instead beneath a precious tree, seated on a throne of celestial raiment;
with a body that is both inferior and superior, he turns the wheel of the Four Noble Truths of non-arising. Furthermore, those of dull faculties outside the realm— [perceive him likewise].

One immediately sees him within the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbhadhatu), seated upon the Flower King Throne, turning the wheel of the four truths in their infinite aspects with his perfect reward body (vipākakāya), even benefiting those of sharp faculties beyond the world-systems.

Furthermore, one immediately sees him dwelling in the Land of Tranquil Light (Śāntaprabhā-bhūmi), seated upon the throne of empty space, turning the wheel of the unconditioned four truths with his pure dharma body (dharmakāya). This is the Buddha-body.
They do not move; yet, because their capacities and insights differ, they are said to be distinguished horizontally.

As for vertical distinction, as in this sutra, the hundreds of thousands of myriads of Śākyamunis sitting beneath the Bodhi tree correspond in meaning to the "Inferior Response" (Lèyìng), which accords with the capacities of those for whom the Tripitaka Teaching is intended.

The Buddha on the Thousand-Petalled Lotus dwells within the palace of the fourth dhyāna. In principle, he corresponds to a "subordinate yet superior" *nirmāṇakāya* (inferior-superior response body), responding to the capacities of those in the Shared Teaching (*sāmānyayāna*).
Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "When a Bodhisattva’s merits are fully perfected, at the realm of Akaniṣṭha, he manifests a body that is the highest and greatest in all worlds;
by means of the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, ignorance is suddenly exhausted. This is called... [the Name].
The wisdom of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) spontaneously possesses inconceivable activity, which is able to manifest throughout the ten directions to benefit sentient beings;

this is its proof. Vairocana Buddha, who personally resides in the Lotus Flower Terrace Treasury World, corresponds in meaning to the *parabhogika-rūpakāya* (body of enjoyment for others), also called the "supreme response-body" (*viśiṣṭa-nirmāṇakāya*).
This responds to the capacities of those following the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavahāra-yāna*). Thus, the Buddha-bodies differ according to their respective locations.

The locations also differ. If those of the *āgama* (Tripitaka) teaching turn their faculties toward the *pāramitā* (Shared) teaching, they leave beneath the tree and come to see the Buddha within the fourth dhyāna.
If those of the *pāramitā* teaching enter into the *vaipulya* (Distinct) teaching, they proceed from the fourth dhyāna back to the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*).
Only those of the Perfect Teaching possess sharp faculties; regarding all bodies, whether horizontal or vertical, they clearly realize them all as...

Since the body of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) manifests immediately, the specific characteristics and location of the physical body are not explained separately; this is what is meant by "vertical discernment. Question:
Since the *Awakening of Faith* belongs to the Perfect and Sudden Mahāyāna, why can its description of the Buddha’s marks be classified as belonging to the Shared Teaching? Answer:

Since the text states that he "manifests the highest and greatest body in the world," we know this refers to a transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya), and does not point to the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) or the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya). As for the Shared Teaching...
This serves as the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna. By first connecting with the Three Piṭakas, it prevents one from lingering in the "transformed city" (the provisional stage);

by subsequently connecting with the Separate and Perfect Teachings, it causes all to return together to the "Jeweled Place" (the ultimate goal). Therefore, it is most appropriate for the Bodhisattva of Perfected Merit to manifest this body, as it perfectly accords with the present sutra.
This is because the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system is unified within the single realm of form.
It pervades the heavens; thus, it also unifies the Buddha-body, which is what is meant by the "thousand Śākyamunis upon the thousand petals surrounding [the central lotus].
Within the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka-dhātu*), it is the most exalted and lofty, and is therefore called the "Supreme Response Body" (*vibhūti-nirmāṇa-kāya*).

In contrast to the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*), it still belongs to the stage of segmented birth (*paricchinna-janman*), and is therefore termed "endowed with inferiority. The phrase "wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment" clarifies that this is the response body.

Regarding the capacities of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao): when it is said that ignorance is suddenly exhausted and termed "all-encompassing wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*), this is from the perspective of the provisional (*upāya*).
It refers to the complete severance of the habitual tendencies of ignorance within both form and mind, which is also designated as the Buddha-eye and all-encompassing wisdom.

From the perspective of the ultimate reality (*tattva*), this refers to the manifestation of the responsive transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*) descending from the Dharma-body and Reward-body. When it is said that inconceivable karma can manifest throughout the ten directions, this is precisely what is meant by...
On a single flower are ten billion lands; in each land is one Śākyamuni. These thousands of billions of Śākyamunis are the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the thousand Śākyamunis.
They exist suddenly where they were previously non-existent. Furthermore, there are two kinds: first, manifesting the form of a Buddha; second, manifesting the forms of the nine realms.
Like Gadgadasvara, Avalokiteśvara, and others, they manifest bodies according to the class of beings. When they come, they are not perceived; when they depart, they are not perceived.
Awakening! The Way of all Buddhas is the same; it is through the resonance of universal compassion that these wondrous functions are accomplished.

Regarding these three bodies (*trikāya*), their meanings are immeasurable, yet they are not distinct entities in essence. The *dharmakāya* is like the substance of a pearl, perfectly round; the *saṃbhogakāya* is like the pure radiance of the pearl;

the *nirmāṇakāya* is like the reflections within the pearl that interpenetrate one another. Without the substance, there is no radiance; without the radiance, there are no reflections. It is by means of these reflections...
O Jñānaprabha, by means of light one perceives the essence; thus the principle of the three bodies is clarified, and the meaning of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* is revealed.
Furthermore, these three bodies are identical to the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*). The Dharma-body is the virtue of the Dharma-body, for apart from the Middle Way there is no separate essence.
The Reward-body is the virtue of Prajñā, because the realization of principle proceeds from true wisdom. The Transformation-body is the virtue of Liberation, as it manifests everywhere.
Because they manifest and appear accordingly, the secret treasury of the three virtues neither increases for the Buddhas nor decreases for sentient beings;

the same applies to the three bodies (*trikāya*). They are simply the three bodies at the stage of principle (*li-ji*) during delusion, and the ultimate three bodies upon the attainment of Buddhahood.
The speaker delights in what is held in their heart, declaring that the Buddhas have long cultivated and long realized the single essence of the three bodies. Thus it is understood.
Knowing that all sentient beings equally possess this virtue, his great compassion permeates his heart, and he constantly contemplates their deliverance.

Now that the conditions and capacities have first ripened, he receives them back to the world of the original source, where they may personally attend upon the Original Honored One and receive the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground.

Subsequently, he again manifests the attainment of enlightenment beneath the tree, universally establishing the heavy and light precepts for ordinary beings, so that those who receive them may achieve sudden [awakening].
Entering the stage of Buddhahood, one becomes a true son of the Buddha; thus, the original aspiration to deliver sentient beings finds fulfillment here.

According to the text, the first fascicle is taught by Vairocana, while the second fascicle is taught by Śākyamuni. However, for this scripture to be transmitted to this world, it must necessarily have been recounted by Śākyamuni.
Therefore, when the title refers to the "Buddha’s teaching," it should be understood as referring to Śākyamuni, who, by virtue of the three bodies (*trikāya*), [is the speaker].

Because they are not different. Question: Since the three bodies (trikāya) are not different, why did Śākyamuni lead the great assembly back to the world of the Lotus-womb Treasury (Padmagarbha-lokadhātu) to worship Vairocana together? Answer: Although the three bodies are not different, they are also not fixedly one;
they are different within their non-difference. Therefore, this is explained according to the vertical perspective, as in this sutra where Śākyamuni [manifests] across billions of lands.
The *śamatha* flower pedestal is one through non-oneness; thus, it is explained in terms of the horizontal dimension.
As in the *Avataṃsaka*, the immovable site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) pervades all dust-like lands.

Furthermore, because it is non-one through oneness, the *Avataṃsaka* clarifies that one may see Śākyamuni, or Amitāyus, or Akṣobhya, or Bhadramukha, and so forth, so as not to fixate upon it as a single, determinate entity.
Regarding this view, because they are different yet not different, this sutra states that these thousands of billions [of forms] are the very body of Vairocana.
This is intended to prevent people from forming a fixed view of difference; since the oneness or difference of the Buddha-body is inconceivable.
The transmission and propagation of the Dharma is likewise inconceivable. That is to say: in the first instance, Vairocana transmits the Dharma, which the thousand Śākyamunis receive;
in the second instance, the thousand Śākyamunis transmit the Dharma, which the hundreds of billions of Śākyamunis receive;
in the third instance, the hundreds of billions of Śākyamunis transmit the Dharma, which all sentient beings receive, continuing even unto the present.
Sentient beings transmit the Dharma from one to another, and subsequent generations receive it in succession.

If one speaks of their differences, then even those who are the same are different; Śākyamuni is not yet the Thousand Buddhas, and the Thousand Buddhas are not yet the Ten Billion Buddhas—how much less so the Hundred Thousand Myriad Buddhas?
How could they be identical to all sentient beings? This is called the "trace" (the manifested form), which is spoken according to [sentient beings'] dispositions. If one speaks of their sameness:

Thus, that which is different is also identical. Since the thousands of billions [of Buddhas] are the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the thousand Buddhas, and the thousand Buddhas are themselves the transformation body of Vairocana, how could all those sentient beings alone not be of the same essence as Vairocana? Therefore it is said:
"If a person receives the Buddha-precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas. You are one who shall become a Buddha; I am one who has already become a Buddha. This is so.
The "Root" (ben) refers to what is taught according to wisdom; it is the root that serves as the trace (ji). Through the trace, the root is revealed.

This signifies the intention of lifting up and receiving the great assembly back into the Lotus Treasury World (*padmagarbha-lokadhātu*). Vairocana is the root, while the thousand Śākyamunis are the traces.
The thousand Buddhas are again the root, while the thousands of billions of Śākyamunis are the traces. These thousands of billions are again the root, and all sentient beings [are likewise so].

The provisional manifestation (*jia*) is for the sake of the ultimate reality (*ben*). Even those who successively transmit the Dharma are again the ultimate reality, while those who receive the Dharma are again the provisional manifestation.
Thus, the ultimate and the provisional are layered upon one another in an inconceivable manner. Yet, apart from the ultimate reality, there is no provisional manifestation;

the provisional is the manifestation of the ultimate's own house. Therefore, it is said: "Sentient beings are within the mind of the Buddhas. Furthermore, apart from the provisional manifestation, there is no ultimate reality; the ultimate is the reality of the provisional's own house. Therefore, it is said: [the ultimate is the reality of the provisional].

The Buddhas within the minds of sentient beings, as well as the *honji-suijaku* (original and trace) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, are arranged vertically across kalpas as numerous as motes of dust;

the *honji-suijaku* of this present sūtra, however, are arranged horizontally across billions of worlds. Vertically, past and present do not depart from the present moment of thought; horizontally, self and other are not separated by even a hair’s breadth.

Taking the original to bestow the trace, wondrous wisdom accords with worldly conditions to reveal the trace and manifest the original; it harmonizes deluded emotions so they return to wisdom—is this not exquisite?
Ah! Furthermore, this sutra does not merely open up the horizontal aspect of the original and the trace to reveal that self and other are not separated;
it also opens up the vertical aspect of the original and the trace to manifest that the nature of things has been thus from all eternity. As stated at the beginning of the lower fascicle:
"I have now come to this world eight thousand times, and for the sake of this Sahā world, I sit upon the Vajra-flower Radiance King throne," and so forth.
In the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara, he has finished briefly expounding the Dharma-gate of Opening the Mind-Ground for the entire great assembly therein.
Is this not the matter of repeatedly manifesting and demonstrating the attainment of Perfect Enlightenment? Therefore, the Lotus Sūtra says:

In truth, the time since I actually attained Buddhahood has been as long as this. However, by means of skillful expedients (*upāya*), I have taught and transformed sentient beings, leading them to enter the Buddha-way, and thus made such statements.

If one were to speak generally of the practice of taking birth and cultivating the bodhisattva path, then upon observing this great earth, there is not even a single mote of dust that is not a place where a bodhisattva has sacrificed their body and life. Furthermore...
How could it have been merely eight thousand times? Question: The opening of the near and the revealing of the far exist only in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;

it is not shared by other sections [of the canon]. Now, since this [present] scripture has only just begun to show the attainment of Buddhahood, how can you immediately take the "revealing of the origin" (*mūlaprakaṭana*) as its interpretation?

Furthermore, if this scripture has already revealed the origin, why would the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* need to reveal it again? Answer: The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* reveals and manifests [the truth] on two occasions, both of which—

This indicates those of provisional capacity within the realm [of the three vehicles], causing them to return to the Buddha-way. This present sutra belongs to the same category as the *Avataṃsaka*; it primarily addresses the two types of capacity beyond the realm.

Even if those of the Two Vehicles were seated here, they would still be like the mute or the deaf; how much more so for those who have not yet been granted a seat at this Dharma assembly—how could they know of this peerless song?
Therefore, one must wait until the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* before the various teachings can be opened and unified. One must not say [otherwise].
Those whose faculties have already matured likewise reach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* before their [understanding] is opened and unified. Question:

Among the Buddha’s three bodies (*trikāya*), which body is it that truly preaches the Dharma? Answer: Since the three bodies are neither identical nor distinct, it is inherently impossible to adhere exclusively to one as being the preacher of the Dharma.

However, because there are differences in the remedies [for specific afflictions], the teachings expounded in the various sūtras differ; some speak of the recompense body (*saṃbhogakāya*) or the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
This is not the true Buddha, nor is it the one who preaches the Dharma. This is intended to prevent people from clinging to appearances and becoming deluded regarding the principle;

therefore, it is shown that the fundamental awakening of the dharma-nature alone constitutes the true Buddha. Some say that the "Dharma-Buddha" refers to the sacred realm of self-awakening, which is beyond words and speech;

thus, the preaching of the Dharma and the manifestation of formal demeanor are all merely the Emanation-Buddha (nirmāṇakāya). This is intended to prevent people from falling into [the error of] [reifying] the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).

In terms of conventional cognition (*sāṃvṛta-pramāṇa*), this refers exclusively to the transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*) manifesting the three wheels [of giving, speech, and action]. In reality, however, preaching the Dharma and saving sentient beings is not the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) alone, yet it does not depart from the Dharma-body.
It is not the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) or the Transformation-body alone, yet it does not depart from the Reward-body or the Transformation-body.

If one grasps the intent of the four *siddhāntas*, one may say that it is the Dharma-body alone that preaches the Dharma; as it is said: "The Reward-body and Transformation-body do not preach the Dharma."

As for this, it may be said that only the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body) preach the Dharma. This is as when it is said that the *dharmakāya* (truth body) is without speech and without preaching.
Alternatively, it may be said that all three bodies together preach the Dharma. This is as when it is said that the *dharmakāya* harmonizes with its merits and manifests everywhere.
It may also be said that each of the three bodies preaches the Dharma individually: the Dharma-body and Reward-body Buddhas preach the Dharma for Bodhisattvas on the stages;

the Supreme Response-body Buddha preaches the Dharma for those prior to the stages, as well as for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; and the Inferior Response-body Buddha preaches the Dharma for all ordinary beings.
Alternatively, it may also be said that the three bodies collectively have nothing to preach, as it is said: "For forty-nine years..."

Not a single word was spoken. If one does not understand the four *siddhāntas* (the fourfold principles) as their underlying causes and conditions, then clinging to even a single phrase is called slandering the Buddha.
Next, the explanation of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* is divided into two parts: first, by way of analogy; second, by way of the Dharma. Regarding the first, the analogy:
the Sūtra says that at that time, the Buddha beheld the net-bannered canopy of the Great Brahmā Kings, and because of this, he spoke of how immeasurable worlds are like...
The mesh of the net: each world is distinct from the others, differing in infinite ways. The gateways of the Buddha’s teaching are likewise so.
Thus, we know that these are names established by means of analogy. That which serves as the analogy is singular—namely, the Brahma-king’s pearl banner.

That which is analogized is twofold: namely, the worlds and the gateways of the Buddha’s teaching. The worlds refer to the sentient beings who are the objects of the teaching; the gateways of the teaching...

This refers to the Dharma that is able to be received. The nature of the Dharma is equal; its principle is not manifold. It is because the capacities [of sentient beings] differ that the gateways of teaching also vary.
Initially, in clarifying those who are to be reached, the term "sentient beings" is not used, but rather "worlds" is employed.

This is to cite the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment) to encompass the *upapatti-vipāka* (the inhabitants). That is to say, from the Buddha-worlds down to the worlds of hell. By means of this kind...
All such worlds are formed by the two types of delusion—common and individual—of sentient beings. Within the common there is the individual, and within the individual there is the common;
as the common and individual mutually condition one another, they establish a network of lands with distinctions of purity and defilement that cannot be fully exhausted by words.
To explain this briefly, there are four kinds of lands: first, the land of eternal quiescent light; second, the land of true retribution without obstruction.
Third is the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder; fourth is the Land of Common Dwelling for Ordinary Beings and Sages. Regarding the inclusion of the ten realms within these four lands:
the Land of Tranquil Light is the world of Buddhas; the Land of True Reward is the world of Bodhisattvas; the Land of Skillful Means is the world of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
and the Land of Common Dwelling is the world of the six ordinary realms. Within each of these four lands, there is further differentiation into the pure and the impure.
[This section] contains both the horizontal and vertical meanings. Now, first the four lands will be explained. First, regarding the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light:

"Eternal" refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); "Quiescent" refers to liberation (*vimukti*); and "Light" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*). Furthermore, all three virtues are eternal because their nature is immutable;
all three virtues are quiescent because they are free from defilement and toil; and all three virtues are light because they are supremely luminous and pure.
These three dharmas—neither vertical nor horizontal—are called the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*). This is the dwelling place of the pure *dharmakāya*.
In terms of wisdom, it is called the "body" (*kāya*); in terms of principle, it is called the "land" (*kṣetra*). Body and land are of one suchness; they do not possess two distinct characteristics.
There is no state of mutual separation here, yet in reality, it pervades throughout all distinct realms and distinct worlds.
The realm (*dhātu*). Because there is no other place for its establishment apart from this.

As for the "True Reward Unobstructed Land," it is the true fruit of retribution realized through cultivation that accords with the nature, arising from the entirety of that nature; therein, matter and mind are sovereign, and atoms and lands mutually contain one another.

It is the dwelling place where the Great Beings (mahāsattvas) of the earth roam; therein the body can manifest the land, and the land likewise manifests the body, without contravening the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Its supreme and wondrous adornments are as fully elucidated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* regarding the Ocean of the Establishment of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-vyavasthāna-samudra*).
As for the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder (*upāya-śeṣa-bhūmi*), it is the realm outside the triple world where the noble multitudes of the three vehicles cultivate the path of skillful means.

As for "abiding," it means that while they have transcended the *pariccheda* (segmented) death, they have not yet avoided the *pariṇāma* (transformative) death; and while they have exhausted the *dṛṣṭi-kleśa* (afflictions of views and thought), they have not yet eliminated the distinct delusions (*bhinna-avidyā*).
Therefore, it is called "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*). This refers to nine types of persons born in this land: two from the *Hīnayāna* (*pitaka*) teachings—the *śrāvaka* and the *pratyekabuddha*;

three from the *Pāramitā* (*sāmānya*) teaching—the *śrāvaka*, the *pratyekabuddha*, and the Bodhisattva of the sixth stage and above; and three from the *Distinct* (*bhinnakrama*) teaching—the [Bodhisattvas of the] ten... [stages].

The stages of Abiding, the Ten Practices, and the Ten Transferences constitute the stage of the Ten Faiths for a person of the Perfect Teaching. Regarding the Land of Common Dwelling of Ordinary Beings and Sages:

the nine stages of the three realms and the twenty-five states of existence are originally summoned and experienced by ordinary beings through their tainted karma—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or imperturbable—and yet sages likewise dwell therein together with them. As for this "common dwelling":

There are two kinds of noble ones: first, the real; second, the provisional. As for the real, these noble ones were originally ordinary beings who, due to the牵引 (karmic attraction) of their past deeds, were born into this realm.
After being born into this realm, they realized the fruits of the Three Vehicles through the power of cultivating the Path.
As for "sovereignty" (*vaśitā*), it refers to these sages who are either inhabitants of the Land of Quiescent Light, the Land of True Reward, or the Land of Expedient Means.
Out of the power of their great compassionate vows, they manifest birth in this realm out of pity for sentient beings; it is not that they are dragged there by karma.

Because these two types of sages dwell together with ordinary beings, it is called the Land of Common Dwelling of Ordinary Beings and Sages. Question: Within the Land of Common Dwelling, as for the sages...

There are provisional and ultimate [teachings]. Within the aforementioned three lands, there are only sages and no ordinary beings; do these likewise each have provisional and ultimate aspects? Answer:

Within the Land of Expedient Means (Upāya-bhūmi), there are two provisional and one ultimate. If one exhausts the afflictions of views and thoughts (dṛṣṭi-kleśa and bhāva-kleśa) within the Land of Common Residence (Sahā-loka-dhātu) and thereby ends birth-and-death in the realm of segmented existence (paricchinna-bhava), one then receives the Dharma-nature body within the Land of Expedient Means—just as the nine types of persons previously explained. In total...

This is called "one reality. If the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Land of Tranquil Light and the Land of True Reward manifest as dwelling in the stage of expedient means (*upāya*) in order to entice those of fixed nature among the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), as well as Bodhisattvas prior to the stages, so that they may enter the correct position (*samyaktva-niyāma*), these are called the "two aspects of expediency.

Within the Land of True Reward, there is one aspect of expediency and one aspect of reality. If those who have attained birth by partially destroying ignorance through the stages of the Separate Teaching or the Dwelling Stages of the Perfect Teaching do so, this is called [the third aspect].

This is what is called the Real. If the Dharma-Buddha of the Land of Tranquil Light manifests the Reward Body for the sake of others to teach all Bodhisattvas so that they may exhaust the source of ignorance, this is called the Expedient.
Within the Land of Tranquil Light, there is only the Real and no Expedient, because it is the place where all Buddhas dwell and roam.
Next, to clarify how the four lands are each divided into pure and defiled: within the Land of Common Residence...
When the five turbidities are slight, the world is pure, such as the World of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī), the World of Wondrous Joy (Abhirati), and so forth.
When the five turbidities are heavy, the world is defiled, such as the present Sahā World and so forth. Furthermore, some worlds are purely pure and without defilement;

some are purely defiled and without purity; some are both pure and defiled; some are both defiled and pure; some transition from purity to defilement; and some transition from defilement to purity. Each [is distinct].

Each is distinct; their differences are immeasurable, all resulting from the karmic retributions of sentient beings, leading to these various gradations as extensively explained in the various sutras.

Within the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-kṣetra*), those who analyze emptiness through clumsy means perceive it as defiled, while those who realize emptiness through skillful means perceive it as pure.
To discuss this in detail, the visions of the nine classes of people become increasingly superior in each successive stage, such that they may also be described as progressively more pure.

Regarding "defilement": within the *sahōkai* (real recompense) land, for those who enter through the sequential threefold contemplation (*sanzen*), it is defiled; for those who enter through the single-mind threefold contemplation (*isshin sanzen*), it is pure.
Within the *jakukō* (tranquil light) land, that which is partially realized is called defiled, while that which is ultimate is called pure.

Question: In the *dōkyō* (shared) land, purity and defilement can be distinguished because one is led there by karma. However, as for the [other] three lands above it, they are all abodes of sages; why, then, would there still be defilement? Answer:

For example, the exquisite beauty of Sundarī, when compared to celestial maidens, is no more than a blind monkey; the finest delicacies of *sūda*, viewed by those in the dhyāna heavens, are no more than pus and blood;
and the wondrous bodies of the form realm, viewed by those in the four formless realms, are worse than festering sores and poison.
To a practitioner of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), when observed with the Dharma-eye, [the Pure Land] appears like one who is deluded or intoxicated.

Taking this as an analogy, how could purity and impurity ever be exhausted? Until one attains the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (Miaojue), impurity will never be fully eliminated, and purity will never reach its ultimate limit.
Therefore it is said: "Each and every world is distinct from the others; their differences are immeasurable. Next, to clarify the horizontal and vertical perspectives: vertically, they emerge...
From the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka-dhātu*), one enters the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*); from the Land of Expedient Means, one enters the Land of Real Reward (*vipāka-bhūmi*);

and from the Land of Real Reward, one enters the Land of Tranquil Light (*śānta-prabhāsa*). Since the severing of delusions varies in depth, the abodes likewise differ vastly in their height and status.

Transversally, without moving from one's current location, what is perceived differs. Within the Land of Common Residence, one may transversally transcend the three lands; that is to say, one perceives—

When the afflictions of thought are severed and exhausted, one sees the land of expedient means (*upāya-bhūmi*). When the dust-like defilements are severed and exhausted, one breaks through ignorance (*avidyā*);

thus one sees the land of true recompense (*vipāka-bhūmi*) and also partially perceives the land of serene light (*śāntaprabhā-bhūmi*). When ignorance is completely severed and exhausted, one clearly perceives the land of serene light.

Within the land of expedient means, one horizontally transcends the two lands—namely, the land of true recompense and the land of serene light. Within the land of true recompense, one horizontally transcends one [land].

The Land refers to the Constant, Quiescent, and Radiant Light (*nitya-praśānta-ābhāsvara*). Within this Land of Constant, Quiescent, and Radiant Light, there is nothing further to transcend, nor is there any distinction between horizontal and vertical dimensions.

Furthermore, with respect to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the noble ones of the Three Vehicles, they exercise mastery over the horizontal and vertical dimensions within their respective lands; this is called the Land of Constant, Quiescent, and Radiant Light.

From within this Land of True Retribution (*sambhoga-kṣetra*), they are able to manifest the three lower lands for the sake of sentient beings. Within the Land of True Retribution, they are able to manifest... for the sake of sentient beings.
In the two lower lands, within the land of skillful means (*upāya-bhūmi*), one can manifest the land of common residence (*sahā-bhūmi*) for the sake of sentient beings.

Furthermore, within the land of common residence, one can manifest the three superior lands for the sake of sentient beings; within the land of skillful means, one can manifest the two superior lands for the sake of sentient beings;
and within the land of true recompense (*vipāka-bhūmi*), one can manifest the land of serene light (*prabhāsvara-bhūmi*) for the sake of sentient beings. Therefore, it is said: "immeasurable worlds."
The realms (*dhātu*) are like the meshes of a net, mutually interpenetrating. Next, the teaching that can respond to these capacities is clarified. The Dharma values what accords with the capacity;
since capacities are myriad and diverse, the Dharma also manifests in a thousand transformations. To speak in general terms, there are four kinds of teachings.

This is truly because sentient beings transmigrate through the two deaths solely due to the two kinds of ignorance—the delusion regarding the True and the delusion regarding the Middle. Regarding the delusion regarding the True...
Therefore, there is segmented birth and death (paricchinna-jarā-maraṇa), for which one must establish the teachings within the realm (dhātu) to deliver beings.
Because they are deluded within [the realm], there is transformative birth and death (pariṇāma-jarā-maraṇa), for which one must establish the teachings outside the realm to deliver them.

Furthermore, these two types of delusion—delusion regarding reality and delusion within the realm—each differ in their degree of gravity. Consequently, those within and outside the realm also each possess differing faculties, whether sharp or dull; specifically, delusion regarding reality is grave.

Those who are dull-rooted within the realm of the conditioned cannot give rise to understanding through the contemplation of analytical emptiness; therefore, the teachings of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) arose.

Those whose delusion regarding the truth is slight and who are sharp-rooted within the realm of the conditioned cannot be suitably reached by the contemplation of essential emptiness; therefore, the teachings of the *Vaipulya* (Shared) arose.
Those who are heavy in their delusion regarding the Middle Way and who are dull-rooted beyond the realm of the conditioned cannot [be reached] by the Contemplation of Successive Stages.
Because their delusions could not be cured by such means, the Distinct Teaching (Bie-jiao) arose.

For those whose delusions were slighter yet still within the state of confusion, and who possessed sharp faculties beyond the boundaries [of the mundane], it was realized that their awakening could not be opened unless through the simultaneous practice of the three contemplations in a single mind; thus, the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao) arose. Regarding these four teachings:
Furthermore, each [of these] has four gates: namely, the gate of existence, the gate of emptiness, the gate of both existence and emptiness, and the gate of neither existence nor emptiness.
Thus, there are four sets of four, totaling sixteen gates. Within these sixteen gates, each further possesses four kinds of *siddhānta* (doctrinal tenets).
That is to say, when sentient beings hear each individual gate, they may obtain the benefit of joy; this is the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly tenet). Or they may obtain...

The benefit of generating goodness is the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint for individuals). The benefit of extinguishing evil is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic remedies).
The benefit of entering into principle is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of ultimate truth). Therefore, it is said that the gates of the Buddha’s teaching are likewise thus.

It is just as the worlds are each different and their distinctions are immeasurable. Furthermore, it is said that these four teachings have four further differences in their modes of transformation (*vyūha*):
they may be taught suddenly (*tadā*), gradually (*anupūrveṇa*), secretly (*rahasya*), or indeterminately (*aniyata*). Regarding sudden teaching:

this means revealing the perfect doctrine (*pariniṣpanna-tattva*) all at once; or, although it may include the distinct [teachings], it is intended primarily for those of great capacity (*mahā-āśaya*), such as the *Avataṃsaka*.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, and others that teach gradually are intended specifically for those of lesser capacity, leading them through provisional means into the ultimate reality.

For example, the *Āgamas* constitute the beginning of the gradual teaching, as they expound only the Tripitaka. The Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras) constitute the middle of the gradual teaching, as they discuss all four teachings, yet the followers of the Two Vehicles receive only general benefit therein.

The Prajñāpāramitā constitutes the end of the gradual teaching; while it incorporates the Shared and Distinct teachings, it primarily expounds the Perfect Teaching, yet the followers of the Two Vehicles [still]...
One merely attains distinct benefits. Regarding the "secret teaching," for this [audience] he teaches the sudden, and for that [audience] he teaches the gradual;

within a single session and with a single voice, each understands differently and remains unaware of the others' interpretations. Regarding the "indeterminate teaching," one attains gradual benefits even within the midst of the sudden teaching.
Within gradual teaching, one attains sudden benefit; the small assists the great, and the great assists the small. Such ritual methods are inconceivably harmonious and inclusive;
thus it is said that the gateways of the Buddha’s teachings are likewise so. They are like immeasurable worlds, illustrated by the metaphor of the mesh of a net, wherein they mutually interpenetrate.
Regarding the four teachings in relation to the four lands and the three Buddhas: [the first is] *Jikō* (Prabhāsa-lokadhātu).

The Dharma-Buddha expounds the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). The Retribution-Buddha expounds the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao). The Superior Response-Buddha of Expedient Means expounds the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
The Inferior Response-Buddha of the Shared Dwelling expounds the Treasury Teaching (Zangjiao). Furthermore, the Dharma-Buddha can fully expound all four teachings;

the Retribution-Buddha can expound three teachings, namely the Treasury, Shared, and Distinct; the Superior Response-Buddha can expound two teachings, namely the Treasury and the Shared; and the Inferior [Response-Buddha]...

The *hīna-nirmāṇakāya* (inferior response-body) should be able to preach only one teaching, namely the Tripiṭaka. Furthermore, when dwelling among the inferior beings under trees, it must fully expound all four teachings, because the faculties and natures of the assembly are diverse.

In the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, the *sādhāraṇa-nirmāṇakāya* (response-body with mixed inferior and superior qualities) preaches only three teachings, because those of the Tripiṭaka vehicle cannot perceive [the fourth].
In the *upāya-kṣetra* (land of skillful means), the Buddha of the *praṇīta-nirmāṇakāya* (superior response-body) merely...

The distinct and perfect teachings (*vyākaraṇa* and *pariniṣpanna*) are taught so that one may perceive the Middle Way; for within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the two types of capacities are both severed from their respective divisions.

Within the land of actual recompense (*sambhoga-kṣetra*), the other-enjoyment recompense (*para-sambhoga-vipāka*) teaches only the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*), so that all bodhisattvas may forever exhaust the source of ignorance.

The self-enjoyment recompense (*ātma-sambhoga-vipāka*) merges with the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) and experiences only true bliss; it is not [accessible] to those from the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samalaṃbuddhi*) downward.
One can see it, yet there is no dharma that can be taught. All that the various bodhisattvas perceive is merely the *paranirmita-vipākaja* (recompense for others' enjoyment).
The *sambhogakāya* of the *dharmadhātu* is solely the realm of the noble wisdom of the Buddhas' self-awakening;

it can no longer be described. Furthermore, the *vipākajñāna* is merged with the *dharmatākāya*, which is free from all marks and pervades all bodies; it is neither something that can be spoken of nor...

It is not that there is no speaking; rather, it is the simultaneous illumination of both speaking and non-speaking. This means that while the self-enjoyment body (svasaṃbhogakāya) is quiescent as it merges with the dharma-body (dharmakāya), this is the meaning of "non-speaking.
Yet, the various response bodies (nirmāṇakāya) arise from the dharma and enjoyment bodies to manifest activity; this is the meaning of "speaking.

Furthermore, it is not merely that the dharma-body is neither speaking nor silent; the simultaneous illumination of both speech and silence constitutes the various bodies, such as the enjoyment and transformation bodies.

Each of these also possesses both the functions of speech and silence. Proclaiming through the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) is called "speech," while entering into meditative absorption (*samādhi-samāpatti*) is called "silence.
Some say that preaching the Dharma benefits sentient beings, whereas remaining silent allows one to personally enjoy the bliss of the Dharma;
this is merely a general statement. Indeed, there are sentient beings who, upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, attain joy and give rise to wholesome roots.

Regarding those who eliminate evil and enter into principle: there are further sentient beings who, upon seeing the Buddha remain silent, attain joy, give rise to wholesome states, eliminate evil, and enter into principle.
For this reason, whether the Tathāgata speaks once or remains silent, it all pertains to the conditions of the four *siddhārtha* (the four purposes).
Furthermore, it is said that through verbal expression, the four teachings and sixteen gates are manifested, such that each gate enables one to attain the four benefits.
Through silence as well, the four teachings and sixteen gates can be revealed, and each gate likewise enables one to attain the four benefits.
If one infers from the spoken teaching, one is initially judged to be a follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*); if one infers from the silence, one is initially judged [to be a follower by dharma].
This is the practice of Dharma. Furthermore, there are those who follow the Dharma by arising from the teaching of the Dharma;
there are also those who follow through faith by arising from silence. These matters are not uniform. Moreover, there are those who grasp the meaning from the state of silence.

Those who grasp the meaning immediately upon hearing the Dharma are, for the time being, judged to be of sharp faculties. Those who require the manifestation of signs through entering meditative concentration are, for the time being, judged to be of dull faculties.
Furthermore, those of sharp faculties awaken upon hearing it once, whereas those of dull faculties must enter meditative concentration for signs to be shown.
Nor is it uniform. Now, to further summarize its meaning according to the capacity of the responsive stimulus (*kai-kan*):

the inferior manifestations (*nyō-ō*) numbering in the hundreds of thousands of myriads beneath the tree were specifically intended to respond to the capacities of those in the *Piṭaka* (Tripitaka) Teaching. Yet, among ordinary beings of the mundane stage (*bokuchi bonpu*), there are those who have from of old possessed the faculties of the Shared, Distinct, and Perfect Teachings;
these individuals hear the latter three teachings even while facing this inferior manifestation. Furthermore, at the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, the inferior and superior [manifestations] coexist.
The Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is primarily intended for those whose faculties correspond to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).

However, among gods and worldlings who have previously possessed the faculties of the Distinct (*viśeṣa*) or Perfect (*sampanna*) Teachings, they hear the latter two teachings while this [Response Body] manifests as an inferior-superior response body.

The Superior Response Body (*upāya-viśeṣa-nirmāṇakāya*) is primarily intended to connect the Shared Teaching to the entry into the Distinct and Perfect Teachings; thus, those of dull faculties hear only the Distinct Teaching, while those of sharp faculties hear both.

Having heard the Perfect Dharma, one encounters the Reward Body upon the lotus throne in the Land of True Reward. This body primarily corresponds to the capacities of those of the Separate and Perfect Vehicles;
thus, while the *Avataṃsaka* is Perfect yet inclusive of the Separate, this sutra is Separate yet inclusive of the Perfect.

Indeed, when Buddhas manifest their bodies and preach the Dharma, it is fundamentally for the sake of the One Reality while employing the three provisional means; they must lead these three provisons back to the One Reality. Since they have already preached the Dharma...

Furthermore, there is guidance by means of signs and guidance through the preaching of the Dharma. Moreover, there are two further meanings: first, vertical guidance; second, horizontal guidance. As for vertical guidance:
first, the *Āśaya* (Aśvaghoṣa) is taught to eliminate ordinary sentiments; next, the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras) is taught to supersede the understandings of the sages;
next, the Prajñāpāramitā is taught to harmonize the teachings; and finally, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is taught to harmonize the persons.
As explained previously, among the three gradual approaches, one obtains only partial benefits; it is only upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that one attains the perfect benefit.
This refers to those of the most dull faculties, who must pass through all five flavors in a vertical progression.

As for the horizontal approach, this refers to the two modes of transformation—Secret and Indeterminate—wherein, according to their respective capacities, [the teaching] may be applied even at the stage of the *Āgamas*.

One awakens to the perfect and eternal. Whether through the Vaipulya (fangděng) or the Prajñāpāramitā, one may immediately awaken to the perfect and eternal; it is not necessary to exhaustively pass through all the flavors.
Whichever flavor one follows, one attains transcendental entry. This is what is meant by: "If poison is placed in milk, the milk itself kills the person.
Whether it be curd, the two types of ghee, or even clarified butter (sarpis), as soon as the poison manifests within them, they all likewise kill the person. Thus it is shown.

There are also two meanings to "inducing by means of signs": first, vertical induction; second, horizontal induction. Vertical induction refers to those whose faculties have matured beneath the tree who attain vision of the body of Akaniṣṭha;
those whose faculties have matured in the four heavens who are received and led back to the Flower Treasury World (Huāzàng);

and those whose faculties have matured in the Flower Treasury World who realize and enter the equal Dharma-nature. Horizontal induction refers to those who, from this very [state of] the sixteen-foot inferior response-body...
When those of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) have matured their faculties, they perceive it as a great, lofty, and supreme response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

When those of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) have matured their faculties, they perceive it as an ocean of marks as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field. When those of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) have matured their faculties, they perceive it as the pure and wondrous Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Regarding these two types of inducement—horizontal and vertical—each further possesses two meanings.

If those sentient beings have not yet subdued or severed the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), the dust-like afflictions (*rajas-kleśa*), or ignorance (*avidyā*), yet are able to see the superior response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the other recompense-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), or the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), this is because their past causes are about to ripen;
thus, the Buddha employs his supernatural powers to empower them so that they may see. Only after seeing do they attain the severance of delusions and the manifestation of principle.
If those sentient beings have already subdued and severed the three delusions and thereby attained the vision of the three bodies, this is because their present merit has matured;
thus, the Buddha responds to them according to their capacities. It is like the moon appearing naturally when the water is clear.

Yet, the Buddha’s power depends upon their own power, and their own power is conditioned by the Buddha’s power. Thus, the path of resonance and response intersects, and the capacity and the Dharma correspond to one another. This is especially so...
One sees that although they are distinct and immeasurable, they mutually interpenetrate. Having concluded the explanation by way of analogy, next is the explanation by way of the Dharma.
The Brahma-net is precisely the nature of the minds of sentient beings;

it is the fundamental source of all Buddhas, the root of practicing the bodhisattva path, and the foundation for all the sons of the Buddha in the great assembly. Its self-nature is inherently pure, and thus it is called "Brahma" (*brahman*).
The inclusion and containment of all dust-like particles is called a "net.

From this nature of mind, there are established the phenomena of immeasurable worlds and sentient beings, as well as the teachings of immeasurable gateways and the dharmas of all Buddhas. Therefore it is said: "Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
Furthermore, the substance of this nature of mind is utterly beyond defilement and purity, yet it is universally capable of giving rise to all things, both defiled and pure.
When phenomena are defiled or pure, they remain neither defiled nor pure. Defilement is the *dharmadhātu*, and purity is also the *dharmadhātu*.

Both defilement and purity are inconceivable; this is what is called "Brahman. That which is called the purity of the Buddha-realm, even down to the purity of the hells, is precisely this mind-nature.
Its essence is neither identical nor different, yet it is universally able to manifest all various marks of identity and difference. This is exactly as it is.
At another time, difference is not the same as non-difference. Difference is also the dharma-realm; sameness is also the dharma-realm.
That both sameness and difference are inconceivable is what is called the "net. This means that the Buddha is the dharma-realm, and all dharmas tend toward the Buddha;
even down to hell being the dharma-realm, and all dharmas tending toward hell. To speak briefly: as for the mind, it does not arise.
...and that is all. When you have even a single thought, the three thousand [realms] are fully present. This means that within a single moment of mind, the ten realms are necessarily complete;
and within each of these ten realms, they must mutually contain one another, thereby forming one hundred realms.

Each of these one hundred realms possesses the ten suchnesses—ranging from "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) and "nature" (*svabhāva*) up to "the ultimate equality of the beginning and the end"—resulting in a total of one thousand suchnesses. Furthermore, regarding the single real dharma...
One thousand. One thousand provisional names, one thousand lands—these together constitute the three thousand [realms].

As for real dharmas, they are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) from those in the hells up to those in the Buddha-realm. As for provisional names, they are the provisional names from the hells up to the Buddha-realm.
As for lands, they are the dependent retributions (*āśraya-vipāka*) from the hells up to the Buddha-realm. Whichever single dharma one points to...

To cite a single name or to pick up any single speck of dust, there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm; principle and phenomena are simultaneously perfected, lacking nothing and having no excess.
As it is with one dharma, so it is with all dharmas; as it is with one name, so it is with all names;
as it is with one speck of dust, so it is with all specks of dust. Yet, it is simply said: "In a mere moment."

Regarding the phrase "The mind contains the three thousand [realms] in their fullness": because sentient beings are too numerous and the Buddha-dharma is too profound, one is first led to contemplate the mind so that awakening and entry may be easier.
Within this very momentary, most subtle, and inferior mind, the natures and characteristics of the three thousand realms are vividly and instantaneously present;
they are neither before nor after, neither decreasing nor increasing. Why is this? Because the essence of a single thought is perfectly complete; this is what is called [the three thousand realms].
This constitutes the "inherently endowed" (li-jù). At the very moment a thought arises, it is termed "phenomenal creation" (shi-zào).
This is because the infinitesimal mind that arises must necessarily fall within one of the ten realms. Once one realm manifests, the other nine realms are simultaneously revealed.
Thus, when the hell realm appears, all phenomena converge upon the hell realm; there is nothing among the ten realms that is not the realm of hell. Furthermore, the hell realm itself can also...
The ten realms arise universally, even until the Buddha-realm manifests; all phenomena then flow toward the Buddha-realm, for there is nothing among the ten realms that is not the Buddha-realm.
Furthermore, the Buddha-realm is likewise able to give rise universally to the ten realms;

such is the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), not the result of forced contrivance. It is precisely because of this infinitesimal thought-instant that one must fully encompass the Dharma-realm as its own substance.

Purity. If the Dharma-body and Wisdom-body are fulfilled, one is an ultimate Buddha, an ultimate Sage, and ultimately pure.
